summary: The build can start: Node.js, npm, the DocumentDB MCP server, and a rich set of DocumentDB skills are available and the live cluster URI is provided via DOCUMENTDB_URI. Key factual confusions were found (most traceable to older Cosmos DB / Mongo API assumptions) but are verifiable and correctable with the installed skills and the Microsoft Learn docs. Missing accelerators (the DocumentDB Agent Kit) and a few developer tools (mongosh, azd, bicep, terraform on PATH) slow iteration but do not block the sample creation; several implementation choices (driver version pins, webhook retry policy, exact schemas and seed data) remain unspecified and must be decided by the builder.
summary_points: Build can proceed: Node.js (v24) and npm are present, the documentdb MCP server is available for verifying collections/indexes/queries, and Microsoft Learn search is available for authoritative facts.

Multiple cold answers reflected Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts / az cosmosdb) or other neighbours; the correct resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and CLI is az documentdb mongocluster (not az cosmosdb).

Connection string format, auth methods, capacity model, local development image/port, vector and full-text search, and change-stream support were clarified using the installed DocumentDB skills and Microsoft Learn pages.
An accelerator (DocumentDB Agent Kit) is missing and would speed building; mongosh and some IaC CLIs are also not on PATH but have workable workarounds (use MCP tools or az commands).
Several implementation decisions are still open (Mongoose/mongodb driver versions, webhook retry semantics, exact schema and seed data); the builder must choose defaults and document them.

tools.name: node / npm
tools.needed_for: Run and build the Node.js sample app, install dependencies, run seed scripts and start the service.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run or build the Node.js sample locally.

tools.name: documentdb (MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Data-plane verification against the live cluster: list databases, create indexes, run aggregation pipelines, sample documents, explain plans, and confirm what the sample created.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server with 18 tools (documentdb_list_databases, documentdb_create_index, documentdb_aggregate, etc.). Must pass connection_profile "default" on calls.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would be unable to programmatically verify collection/index state or run live aggregations through the agent; manual verification would be slower.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh or the Azure portal to inspect the cluster manually; however mongosh is not on PATH in this inventory.

tools.name: learn_microsoft_docs_search
tools.needed_for: Authoritative Microsoft Learn docs and quickstarts to verify product facts (resource types, CLI commands, supported features, sample connection strings).
tools.detail: Microsoft Learn search and fetch tools are available in MCP (learn_microsoft_docs_search & fetch).
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder would lack authoritative docs to ground design choices; increased risk of using obsolete guidance.
tools.workaround: Fall back to installed DocumentDB skills for many facts; but Microsoft Learn pages are the canonical references.

tools.name: documentdb-azure-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: Authoritative deployment facts: resource provider namespace and resource type (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters), Bicep/Terraform mapping, connection-string form, compute tiers, and CLI examples for creating clusters.
tools.detail: Installed skill with detailed deployment and CLI examples. States resource-type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and sample connection-string format.
tools.impact_if_missing: Hard to know the correct resource type and CLI commands for cluster lifecycle; builder might try az cosmosdb or databaseAccounts accidentally.
tools.workaround: Use Microsoft Learn quickstarts, but this skill packages the relevant deployment guidance.

tools.name: documentdb-connection (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver connection best practices, TLS requirement, recommended options for MongoClient, singleton pattern, and pool tuning for Node.js.
tools.detail: Installed — provides code patterns (singleton MongoClient), required TLS and options, and pool sizing guidance.
tools.impact_if_missing: Risk of bad connection patterns (per-request clients), timeouts and pool misconfiguration causing production failures.
tools.workaround: Follow generic MongoDB driver docs, but this skill tailors settings to DocumentDB peculiarities.

tools.name: documentdb-driver (skill)
tools.needed_for: Driver-level best practices (singleton client pattern) and guidance on Mongoose / mongodb usage.
tools.detail: Installed — short driver best-practice rules and resources.
tools.impact_if_missing: Higher chance of connection churn and pool exhaustion in the sample.
tools.workaround: Follow upstream MongoDB driver docs; but the skill provides DocumentDB-specific caveats.

tools.name: documentdb-local-deployment (skill)
tools.needed_for: If the builder wants to run a local DocumentDB gateway container for tests (image name and port, TLS hints and env flags).
tools.detail: Provides the recommended local gateway image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) and the Mongo wire port 10260 for the gateway.
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to provide a local dev environment that mirrors the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Work against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as the run environment instructs; Docker is present so local Gateway could be run by installing the image.

tools.name: documentdb-vector-search (skill)
tools.needed_for: Vector index and vector-search guidance (DiskANN / HNSW / IVF), but only relevant if the sample wants to demonstrate vector indexes or $search hybrid queries.
tools.detail: Installed — documents cosmosSearch vector types and recommended index subtypes.
tools.impact_if_missing: Builder might miss DocumentDB's built-in vector-search features and incorrectly integrate an external vector store.
tools.workaround: Use application-side vector search or Azure Cognitive Search, but this is slower and requires extra infrastructure.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Optional: inspect or manage Azure resources, verify provider registration, and run az-based deployment snippets provided by the deployment skill.
tools.detail: az is installed and signed in (azure-cli 2.89.1); cosmosdb/documentdb related extensions present in extensions list.
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run az-based deployment snippets or confirm provider registration; limited to portal/manual checks.
tools.workaround: Use the documentdb MCP tool or Microsoft Learn instructions for resource references; the sample does not need to provision new clusters for run.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run a local DocumentDB Gateway container for local integration testing.
tools.impact_if_missing: No local container-run option; must test against the live cluster.
tools.workaround: Test directly against the live cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as the skill_md instructs.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) — not installed; would accelerate scaffolding, sample code snippets, and conventions for sample apps.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (sometimes shown as databaseAccounts).
confusions.grounded_answer: Provider namespace is Microsoft.DocumentDB and the correct resource type for the managed DocumentDB cluster is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not databaseAccounts).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace and historical overlap: older Cosmos DB (the 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB' or 'vCore' offering) used Microsoft.DocumentDB databaseAccounts in some ARM templates; callers and older docs still reference databaseAccounts.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb commands would target the Cosmos DB account API or create the wrong resource type, causing deployment/management failures or inconsistent runtime behaviours.
improvements: Update deployment quickstarts and the developer README to state explicitly: use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (az documentdb mongocluster) when provisioning Azure DocumentDB clusters rather than databaseAccounts/az cosmosdb.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in Azure CLI group 'az cosmosdb' ... This is in the core set of CLI commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: Use the az documentdb mongocluster command group (e.g., az documentdb mongocluster create / az documentdb mongocluster show); the CLI surface provides az documentdb commands for mongoClusters.

grounding_links.title: Quickstart: Create an Azure DocumentDB cluster by using Azure CLI

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Legacy and neighbouring product documentation (Cosmos DB's az cosmosdb) describe Mongo API operations under az cosmosdb; the new mongoClusters resource uses a new az documentdb command group.

confusion_sources.title: Examples and older Cosmos DB docs referencing az cosmosdb

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb will not create the new mongoClusters resource and could cause the developer to attempt the wrong deployment path or create the wrong account type.
improvements: Add an explicit note to migration and quickstart docs that 'az documentdb mongocluster' is the correct command group for DocumentDB clusters and that az cosmosdb targets the older Cosmos DB account resources.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts ... Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account
confusions.grounded_answer: Bicep/Terraform should target Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (the mongoClusters resource); the Terraform AzAPI / provider surfaces use azurerm_mongo_cluster or an azapi resource targeting Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters in current examples and templates.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Cosmos DB quickstarts and Terraform module names (azurerm_cosmosdb_account) describe Cosmos DB accounts; the new DocumentDB cluster API uses a dedicated mongoClusters resource.
confusions.build_risk: Using databaseAccounts or azurerm_cosmosdb_account templates will not create the expected mongoClusters resource and may produce incompatible accounts.
improvements: Document and surface the correct Bicep and Terraform resource names (Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and azurerm_mongo_cluster or AzAPI use) in the sample's README and deployment notes.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical MongoDB URI for Azure Cosmos DB (Mongo API): mongodb://<username>:<password>@<accountName>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<accountName>@
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB cluster connection strings typically use the SRV form (mongodb+srv://) with host names like <cluster>.global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com (service-specific suffix) and driver options TLS/tls=true (SCRAM-SHA-256), retryWrites=false, and other driver tuning flags. The host suffix and SRV pattern differ from the older cosmos mongo.* host and port 10255; use the connection string retrieved from the cluster's 'Connection strings' view.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB (Mongo API) connection string used .mongo.cosmos.azure.com and TLS ports like 10255; DocumentDB uses a recent SRV-style host suffix (global.mongocluster.cosmos.azure.com) and the SRV scheme in many examples.
confusions.build_risk: Using the wrong host suffix or port will cause connection failures; hardcoding the wrong URI format will block local runs and tests.
improvements: Show the exact connection-string example used by the cluster in the sample README and point developers to the cluster 'Connection strings' UI or az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings command.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Azure Cosmos DB typically charges by Request Units (RUs/sec); newer vCore surface exists but standard is RUs or serverless.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is billed on compute tiers (vCore-like 'M' tiers, e.g., M10..M200) and storage; it is not provisioned in RUs. The DocumentDB cluster model uses tiered compute (M10, M30, etc.) and independent storage sizing.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing and tiers)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Confusion arises because Cosmos DB (Core/NoSQL) historically uses RUs, and some Cosmos Mongo variants presented both RU and vCore surfaces; DocumentDB uses M-tier compute sizing instead.
confusions.build_risk: Designing for RUs (or thinking throughput quotas are set per container) will cause the developer to pick the wrong resources and misunderstanding of cost/scale behaviour.
improvements: State in the sample README that the target cluster uses compute tiers (M10/M30/etc.) and link to the DocumentDB pricing page and the deployment skill which documents compute tiers.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: For the MongoDB API the primary supported auth is username/password ... Azure AD (Microsoft Entra) data-plane authentication is not generally available for the MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native (username/password) authentication and Microsoft Entra ID (Azure AD) data‑plane authentication; cluster creation and configuration expose auth modes (e.g., --auth-allowed-modes can include MicrosoftEntraID). The driver-side Entra flows require using the supported authentication mechanism and the cluster's documented configuration (managed identities or Entra-enabled auth).
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older Mongo API variants or older Cosmos offerings lacked Entra data-plane auth; new DocumentDB supports Microsoft Entra ID and the deployment CLI exposes allowed auth modes.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming only username/password auth is available prevents implementing or documenting Entra-based authentication options; conversely, assuming Entra is always configured will break if the cluster was created with only native auth.
improvements: Add a short 'Authentication' section in the sample README instructing how to verify the cluster's auth modes (portal or az documentdb mongocluster show) and how to choose native vs Entra auth for local runs.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (e.g., mongoose or mongodb). There is not a separate service-specific MongoDB driver.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use the standard MongoDB drivers and ODMs like Mongoose for Node.js; there is no separate service-specific MongoDB driver for Azure DocumentDB. Use DocumentDB-specific driver tuning guidance from the documentdb-connection / documentdb-driver skills.

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB's MongoDB API did not provide built-in vector-index types ... therefore there is no native createIndex(...) vector syntax I would rely on.
confusions.grounded_answer: Incorrect — Azure DocumentDB provides a built-in vector index feature (cosmosSearch) with subtypes (vector-diskann, vector-hnsw, vector-ivf). The documentdb-vector-search skill documents DiskANN/HNSW/IVF choices and the cosmosSearch query syntax used in $search.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many MongoDB-compatible clouds did not originally include vector-index types; older assumptions and Cosmos DB-era docs led to the expectation that vector search needs an external store.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes no native vector index, they might add an external vector store and extra integration complexity unnecessarily.
improvements: Document the DocumentDB vector index capability and give one example in the sample README (or a separate sample) showing how to declare a vector index and run a $search with cosmosSearch.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Use MongoDB text indexes or integrate Cosmos DB with Azure Cognitive Search for richer hybrid / semantic search.
confusions.grounded_answer: DocumentDB provides a native full-text search via createSearchIndexes and the $search aggregation stage (BM25) and supports hybrid retrieval combining BM25 + vector search. You do not have to use Azure Cognitive Search for typical full-text or hybrid scenarios.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Many MongoDB setups rely on Mongo text indexes or an external search service; older Cosmos-based patterns recommended Azure Cognitive Search, causing builders to miss the native createSearchIndexes / $search pathway.
confusions.build_risk: Choosing an external search pipeline increases complexity and cost; the app may not leverage DocumentDB's integrated search score and hybrid features.
improvements: Add sample code and a short example in README showing createSearchIndexes + $search for a simple full-text query as an alternative to a separate search service.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Cosmos DB's MongoDB API supported specific older versions (3.6, 4.0, 4.2) and not all features; check account's server-version.
confusions.grounded_answer: Outdated: Azure DocumentDB supports MongoDB wire protocol versions 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and 8.0 (learn pages list support for 5.0–8.0). The product supports the vast majority of MongoDB operators (documented compatibility tables); administrative commands or a few corner-case operators may differ and should be validated with the compatibility reference.

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB - MongoDB compatibility and supported wire protocol versions
MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Older documentation and older Cosmos DB Mongo API compat notes referenced earlier MongoDB versions; the platform has advanced to support 5.0–8.0 wire protocol versions.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming only older wire versions are supported may cause the builder to pin older drivers unnecessarily or to avoid using modern Mongo features that are available.
improvements: Add an explicit note in sample README to test feature compatibility against the target cluster and link to the Microsoft 'MongoDB compatibility' reference.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator for local development (it supports the MongoDB API) and a Mongo endpoint on port 10250/10255.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB, the recommended local dev option is the DocumentDB Gateway Docker image (ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local:latest) which exposes the MongoDB protocol on port 10260 (with TLS). The Cosmos DB Emulator is a different product and not the DocumentDB local gateway.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB emulator and DocumentDB local gateway are different local tooling; older guidance referencing Cosmos emulator led to the incorrect assumption.
confusions.build_risk: Attempts to start the wrong emulator or connecting to the wrong port will waste developer time and cause local tests to fail.
improvements: In the sample README, explicitly list the Gateway Docker image and the default Mongo port 10260 for local testing, and show example docker-compose snippets from the local-deployment skill.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams availability depends on the MongoDB wire/server version the Cosmos account is configured for; there is no single toggle.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported in Azure DocumentDB. For multishard clusters you may need to enable a 'Change streams for multishard clusters' preview/feature flag in the cluster settings; for standard single-shard usage change streams are available. Documentation provides examples of watch()/Model.watch() usage and resume semantics.

grounding_links.title: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB (Model.watch guidance)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Change-stream support historically varied by account type and wire-version; the current DocumentDB service supports change streams but multishard clusters may require an explicit feature enablement.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes change streams are unavailable, they may implement inefficient polling; if they assume no feature toggle is needed for multishard, they may experience missing events on those clusters.
improvements: Document the exact preconditions for change streams in the sample README and include a small 'verify-change-streams' snippet using the documentdb MCP server to check the cluster settings.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: I believe the service-specific MCP server is 'documentdb' ... the general Azure MCP server can enumerate metadata but the 'documentdb' MCP server provides specialized commands.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides the data-plane tools (list databases, aggregate, list/create indexes, explain, sample documents). The general azure MCP server covers control-plane tasks and best-practice lookups but not data-plane collection inspection.
confusions.grounding_source: machine inventory (documentdb MCP) and documentdb-mcp-setup skill

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Microsoft originally shipped a service named DocumentDB which later evolved and was rebranded as Azure Cosmos DB; the open-source DocumentDB is unrelated.
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly wrong/ambiguous: the branding history is nuanced. 'DocumentDB' was historically the name Microsoft used for an earlier document database product that later became Cosmos DB (SQL/Core). The new managed Mongo-compatible service is branded Azure DocumentDB and supersedes a vCore-based Cosmos-for-MongoDB naming; the open-source DocumentDB engine is the engine behind Azure DocumentDB and is governed by the Linux Foundation — it is related, not unrelated. In short: the naming overlap with 'DocumentDB' and 'Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' causes confusion; the current product is Azure DocumentDB (mongoClusters) and is distinct from Amazon DocumentDB and older Cosmos DB account types.
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple renames and the reuse of the 'DocumentDB' and 'Cosmos DB' names over time; older docs and blog posts refer to the vCore/cosmos variants.
confusions.build_risk: Developers may follow docs for a different product (Cosmos DB account vs mongoClusters) and pick incompatible management paths or assume features that belong to a different product.
improvements: Add a short 'Naming and compatibility' paragraph in the sample README that explicitly explains the current product name (Azure DocumentDB), the old vCore/Cosmos naming, and common neighbours (Amazon DocumentDB, Cosmos DB for NoSQL).

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is Microsoft Azure Cosmos DB's proprietary distributed storage engine providing the MongoDB wire protocol compatibility layer.
confusions.grounded_answer: Wrong: Azure DocumentDB runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine (the microsoft/documentdb project) and in some references is described as built on a PostgreSQL-based engine variant; the important point: applications use the MongoDB wire protocol and standard Mongo drivers, but there are platform differences (admin command exclusions, some operator differences) documented in the compatibility docs.

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Confusion between Cosmos DB's proprietary engine and the open-source DocumentDB engine that powers the new DocumentDB service, plus historical branding that mixed DocumentDB and Cosmos names.
confusions.build_risk: Wrong assumptions about engine internals could lead developers to expect Cosmos DB behaviors (e.g., RU billing) or to copy inapplicable operational guidance.
improvements: Clarify in the sample README that the service runs the open-source DocumentDB engine and that applications use standard MongoDB drivers but must validate operator compatibility against the compatibility matrix.

confusions.question: Which database name does this sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the database named 'sample_fintech_03' for all collections and queries; create/use it explicitly in code: const db = mongoose.connection.useDb('sample_fintech_03');
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment (skill_md) specifies using database sample_fintech_03 for the sample; code should use mongoose.connection.useDb('sample_fintech_03') or connect to it explicitly.

confusions.question: How will the sample read the connection string and connect from Node.js (concrete command/syntax)?
confusions.cold_answer: Read the URI from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and connect with Mongoose: const uri = process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI; await mongoose.connect(uri, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true });
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct pattern: read the cluster URI from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI and connect with Mongoose/MongoClient, ensuring TLS and recommended driver options; do not log the URI and provide .env.example for placeholder.

confusions.question: How should the app open a change stream on the positions collection in Node.js / Mongoose?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the native collection watch API: const coll = mongoose.connection.db.collection('positions'); const changeStream = coll.watch([], { fullDocument: 'updateLookup' }); changeStream.on('change', doc => { /* evaluate alerts */ });
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: using collection.watch or Model.watch with fullDocument:'updateLookup' (or appropriate options) is the recommended approach; check cluster change-stream settings for multishard clusters.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-connection and Microsoft Learn Mongoose tutorial

grounding_links.title: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB: Build a Node.js inventory API

confusions.question: What aggregation pipeline will compute portfolio P&L and sector allocation?
confusions.cold_answer: Example aggregation pipeline (group by symbol -> compute marketValue/cost/pnl -> group to total and bySector -> compute percentages).
confusions.grounded_answer: Partly correct: the pipeline structure the cold answer gave is reasonable and can compute total P&L and per-sector allocations; the builder should test it against sample data and use $group/$project/$unwind stages as needed. The documentdb-natural-language-querying skill and aggregation support in DocumentDB accept such pipelines.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-natural-language-querying skill (availability) and general aggregation support
confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The exact field names the builder chooses will affect the pipeline (e.g., 'shares' vs 'quantity', 'currentPrice' vs 'marketPrice'), so the pipeline must be adjusted to the actual schema; the given pipeline is a good starting point.
confusions.build_risk: If the pipeline is run unchanged against a schema with different field names, results will be wrong; the builder must align field names and ensure numeric types are present.
improvements: Provide a canonical sample schema and a test seed dataset so the aggregation pipeline in the README matches the actual document fields used by the sample.

confusions.question: What indexes should the sample create for good change-stream and alert performance and what are the createIndex commands?
confusions.cold_answer: Create indexes on fields used for queries: db.positions.createIndex({ symbol: 1, updatedAt: -1 }); db.positions.createIndex({ accountId: 1 }); db.alerts.createIndex({ symbol: 1, threshold: 1 });
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct as guidance: indexes on userId/accountId, symbol, and updatedAt are appropriate; create compound index { userId:1, symbol:1 } for common lookups. Change streams themselves do not require special indexes, but alert-evaluation queries should be indexed for performance.

information_gaps.title: Driver version compatibility
information_gaps.description: The sample must pick exact Mongoose and mongodb driver versions compatible with the cluster's MongoDB wire protocol (sample environment mentions MongoDB 7.0). No skill gave a concrete package version to pin; lookups attempted: documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection skills (guidance only).

information_gaps.title: Webhook delivery/retry policy
information_gaps.description: The prompt does not specify how webhook delivery failures should be handled (single fire-and-log, retries with backoff, durable delivery queue). No installed skill prescribes a sample policy; the builder must choose and document it, or consult product policy.

information_gaps.title: Exact Mongoose schemas / field names
information_gaps.description: The prompt leaves the Position and AlertRule field definitions to the builder. No skill supplied an exact field list to use in sample code; the builder must decide canonical field names (shares/quantity, avgCost/currentPrice, sector, userId, webhookUrl, active, etc.).

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset contents and idempotency pattern
information_gaps.description: No installed resource gave a concrete sample dataset or pattern for idempotent seed scripts; documentdb-local-deployment offered best practices but not a seed file. The builder must design a small idempotent seed and document how to re-run it safely.

information_gaps.title: Webhook payload schema and delivery status storage
information_gaps.description: No skill prescribed the webhook HTTP payload shape or whether delivery attempts/status should be persisted; the builder must decide (and may optionally create a 'webhook_deliveries' collection).

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use the DocumentDB cluster resource type Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters and the az documentdb mongocluster CLI group (or the documentdb-azure-deployment skill) — do not use databaseAccounts or az cosmosdb for provisioning.

Read the connection string from process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI at runtime and use the SRV-style connection string provided by the cluster (do not hardcode host suffixes/ports). Ensure TLS is enabled and use driver options recommended by documentdb-connection (singleton MongoClient, retryWrites=false where recommended).

Do not assume RU-based billing or az cosmosdb provisioning; plan for compute-tier (M10..M200) resource sizing and use the documentdb-azure-deployment skill or the pricing docs when describing resource expectations.
If you implement full-text or vector search in the sample, use DocumentDB's native createSearchIndexes and $search (cosmosSearch) features rather than an external search pipeline for the demo.

Open change streams with fullDocument: 'updateLookup' on the positions collection (collection.watch or Model.watch) and verify the cluster's change-stream settings for multishard clusters before relying on it in production.

sources.title: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB (Model.watch guidance)

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this Node.js sample; azd helps scaffold app + infra but the run environment forbids provisioning new clusters. If the team wants the full deploy flow included, instruct builders to install azd (https://learn.microsoft.com/azure/developer/azure-developer-cli/install).

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Bicep is useful for infra-as-code templates but provisioning is out of scope (azure_writes_allowed=false). If a builder wants to run the deploy script locally, they should install bicep; otherwise include the Bicep files in the repo and document how to run them later.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Terraform helps customers who prefer Terraform, but it's not necessary to build the Node.js sample. If desired, add Terraform examples to the repo and instruct users to install terraform via upstream docs.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for a Node.js sample. If the team wants to provide cross-language samples (C#), install dotnet runtime/SDK on the build machine.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Install mongosh for local manual checks and ad-hoc queries against the cluster (useful when the documentdb MCP server is not sufficient). Install via the MongoDB download page or package manager; otherwise rely on the documentdb MCP server tools for data-plane inspection.
